Each linked primary source and necessary followup was inspected live for the particular claims.

evidence.quote: Complete old or new bytes is one guarantee; retaining both is another.

mechanisms.reason: Objectives object-and-key and store-and-retrieve establish actors, state and reference retrieval before whole-object-replace and read-and-list-limits. Lost-response connects completion, observations and guarded writes; durability-versus-success separates storage state from response delivery. Access-boundary and placement-and-split explain concrete consequences.

evidence.quote: The object upload and database commit are separate operations. The object store does not commit them together.

coherence.reason: All eight card objectives and prerequisite edges are satisfied in order: model, two writes, replacement, read/list, uncertainty, recovery, permission boundary, workload synthesis. Diagrams at zero-based indexes 1 and 4 depict separate publication and uncertain/condition-rejected states without invented atomicity. No recurring story is required.

evidence.quote: Publishing a reference is a separate decision from storing the bytes.

decisions.reason: Ready publication/recovery, read-versus-index choice, configured retention and placement, constrained credentials and workload selection are actionable. Conditional writes expose their limited protection. Card 8 contrasts object request/replacement costs with database, block, shared-file and CDN roles.

evidence.quote: Whole-object replacement and request overhead make it a poor default for frequent small in-place edits.

clarity.reason: Bucket/key/prefix, metadata, retention, conditional write and alternative storage interfaces are explained for the stated HTTP/database prerequisites. Diagram captions and accessible labels reinforce the text. Shared LessonDialog and relevant CSS inspected once: index mapping, labeled navigation, prose rendering, source links, scrollable viewport and two-column diagrams are consistent; no browser execution claimed.

evidence.quote: The bucket and key locate an object; the application gives its bytes meaning.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria supported: learner defines bucket/object/key and content-type metadata; scopes flat prefixes and non-atomic rename; separates application fields; traces upload/reference/key read; requires confirmed-ready versus pending publication; explains orphan/missing-byte failures and application recovery without listing transactions.
All three criteria supported: complete same-key replacement; S3/GCS old-or-new concurrent read and new current object; no implicit retention, configured versions and provider-scoped operations.

All four criteria supported: exact key versus prefix versus indexed field query and growing request/data/latency cost; scoped S3/GCS strong read/list consistency with possible failures; pagination is not a frozen transaction; overlapping response arrival does not determine final state.

All three criteria supported: lost response allows completed write and unconditional overwrite; intended identity/content must be established rather than key existence, with later-read provenance limits; conditional absence/version checks protect only specified state, rejection proves no intended upload, lost conditional response remains uncertain and APIs vary.

All three criteria supported: intact retention versus requested accessibility and server completion versus received acknowledgment; redundancy and placement-specific zone failure; overwrite/delete recovery needs enabled, effective, still-retaining protections.

All seven criteria supported: service credential versus application ownership authorization; identifier versus permission and limited trusted credential scope; provider-specific propagation; object whole-upload tradeoff without minimum size; records/query/transaction database; block versus shared-file interfaces; CDN copies near users versus durable origin.

sourceChecks.claim: Inspected AWS object-key flat namespace and console prefix rules; GCS objects followup explicitly describes non-atomic copy/delete of simulated folders. Bucket/key identity and metadata distinction are consistent with the documented model.

Inspected AWS S3 overview object model and key-based atomicity limits. Application/database publication ordering is a valid deduction from the separate actors and commits; listing cannot join them into a transaction.

Inspected GCS objects immutability and atomic replacement passage, AWS overview single-key old-or-new reads, and GCS versioning disabled/soft-delete-disabled replacement table. Complete replacement and separately configured retention are supported.

Inspected GCS consistency read/list, retryable failure and HTTP-cache passages; AWS overview concurrent response ordering and no multi-key atomicity; GCS objects.list pageToken explains additions behind the cursor are omitted. Access paths and scoped consistency claims are supported.

Inspected GCS request-preconditions generation match, zero/live-object absence, 412 and network-race passages, plus AWS conditional-writes If-None-Match and If-Match. Conditions protect the targeted state; a failed condition identifies no successful caller upload, and lost acknowledgment remains uncertain.

Inspected GCS availability-durability definitions, redundancy-before-confirmation and zonal loss warning; AWS data protection redundancy and separate versioning; GCS versioning retention, expiry/deletion and propagation. Completion versus received response remains a separate transport event.

Inspected GCS IAM principals, role permissions and resource scope; GCS consistency access-revocation propagation passage. A broad service principal is distinct from the application user, so application ownership checks remain necessary.

Inspected AWS block/file/object comparison interfaces and database block workload; CloudFront introduction explains cached edge copies and S3 definitive origin. Whole-object versus small-range access and separate database/CDN roles are supported.
